PART 3 — The Revenge Menu: What People Do to Feel Better

3.1 The Many Forms of Revenge

FormWhat it looks likeWhat it is trying to meet
Direct retaliationInsults, counterattack, threats, violenceRestore power and respect
Exposure in returnLeaking messages or screenshots, posting online, "calling out" or cancelling someoneRestore honour by lowering theirs
Relational sabotageGossip, smear campaigns, triangulation, turning children, friends or a congregation against themBelonging and allies; safety in numbers
Passive aggression and withdrawalSilent treatment, withholding help or affection, deliberate lateness, sarcasm, "forgetting"Power without confrontation
Punishing through systemsWeaponised complaints, legal harassment, financial leverage, reporting to authorities out of spiteControl and "justice" — distinguished from legitimate process by motive (see 5.6)
Internal revengeRehearsing comebacks, revenge fantasies, rumination, delighting in their misfortune (schadenfreude)Control, processing, imagined justice
"Success as revenge""I'll show them"; building a life mainly to prove the offender wrongVindication of worth — yet the offender remains the audience
Displaced revengeTaking it out on safer people: spouse, children, subordinates, a proxy groupDischarge of pain where it is safe to do so
Spiritual revenge"God will get you"; praying curses; shunning "in the name of holiness"; using Scripture as a weaponMoral high ground and a divine ally
Self-directedSelf-punishment, self-neglect or self-harm, sometimes to "make them feel guilty" or regain a sense of controlControl, expression of pain, a wish to be seen

If self-directed harm is part of your story, please contact a professional or a crisis line, or your local emergency number (112 in India), promptly. Pain deserves help and a witness, not another injury.

3.2 Why Revenge Feels Like It Will Work

Revenge is not irrational nonsense; it is driven by real wiring. Neuroimaging work (de Quervain and colleagues, 2004, Science) found that anticipating punishing a rule-breaker activated a reward-related region of the brain. Wrongs also leave us feeling powerless, and retaliation promises power; they leave us feeling unseen, and retaliation promises that the offender will finally "get it." Deep down, many people also believe revenge brings closure.

3.3 Why It Doesn't

In three studies, Carlsmith, Wilson and Gilbert (2008, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology) found that people expected punishing a rule-breaker to feel good, but those who actually punished felt worse than those who had no chance to punish — in part because punishers went on thinking about the offender, while non-punishers moved on. Related research links vengefulness with greater rumination and distress. This is one experiment (a laboratory game, a modest wrong), not a verdict on every situation, but it matches what Scripture and pastoral experience have long observed.

Why revenge fails the victimExplanation
It keeps the offender centralRevenge is a project about them; the avenger's life orbits their enemy (this is the "tether" in Part 3.1's "success as revenge").
It prolongs ruminationReplaying and planning keeps the stress response running (see the physiology of grudges in the heart-healing study).
It rarely produces the longed-for acknowledgmentWhat the victim wanted was truth, acknowledgment and safety; retaliation seldom delivers any of these, and often invites a counter-strike.
It spreads the injuryFeuds escalate; Lamech's "seventy-sevenfold" revenge (Gen 4:23-24) shows the logic of escalation.
It changes who we becomeThe avenger risks becoming what he hated; "do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good" (Rom 12:21).

3.4 When the Urge Comes: A Practical Protocol

  1. Name the urge without acting on it. An urge is not a sin ("Be angry and do not sin," Eph 4:26); the act is where the choice lies.
  2. Write the unsent letter. Say everything; do not send it. Burn it or keep it for a safe person to hear.
  3. Wait 24 hours before any message, post or action that is about them.
  4. Run the motive test (5.6): repair and protection, or their pain?
  5. Tell one safe person exactly what you feel like doing.
  6. Lament aloud to God (Psalm 109 and Psalm 137 model bringing raw vengeful longing to God rather than acting on it).
  7. Redirect the energy toward legitimate protection and restoration steps.
  8. When you are ready — not before — pray for their awakening (Matt 5:44), not as a performance but as a slow turning of the heart.

PART 4 — Why We Justify Ourselves

4.1 The Many Faces of Self-Justification

JustificationExampleUsed by
"They started it / they deserved it""After what she did, anything I say is fair."Victims justifying revenge; offenders justifying harm
Minimising"It wasn't that bad."Offenders; also victims protecting a relationship
Comparison"Others do much worse."Both
Good intentions"I only meant to help."Offenders
Moral licensing"After all I've done for you..."Both
Blame-shifting"You made me do it."Offenders (Gen 3:12-13)
Claiming victimhood"I'm the real victim here."Offenders when confronted
Spiritualising"God told me" / "this is discipline" / "it's God's will."Both; especially in religious settings
Technicalities"I never technically lied."Offenders
Future promise"I'll make it up to you someday."Offenders postponing accountability

4.2 What Is Going On Underneath

  • Cognitive dissonance (Festinger, 1957): holding "I am a good person" together with "I did something harmful" is uncomfortable, and the mind relieves the tension most easily by changing the interpretation of the act rather than the self-image. Tavris and Aronson's Mistakes Were Made (But Not by Me) describes how small self-justifications compound step by step, like walking down a pyramid.
  • The I-am-not connection. If worth is believed to depend on being good, right or blameless, then admitting fault feels like confirming "I am bad." The self-justifier is guarding an I-am-not (Kruger's methods 1 and 3: self-salvation and denial/blame).
  • Shame versus guilt. Psychologist June Tangney's research distinguishes shame ("I am bad") from guilt ("I did something bad"): shame-proneness is generally associated with defensiveness, blame and anger, while guilt-proneness is associated with empathy and repair. This is why the shame work in earlier studies in this series is a precondition for honest accountability.
  • It protects victims too. A wronged person may justify revenge because admitting "I want them to suffer, and that is not healing me" is painful.

4.4 The Word "Justify" — and the Gospel's Answer

WordLanguageMeaningWhere
צָדַק tsadaqHebrewTo be righteous; (in the causative) to declare righteous, to vindicateGen 15:6; Isa 53:11
δικαιόω dikaiooGreekTo declare righteous, to put in right standing; the same verb is used when people "justify themselves"Luke 16:15 (self-justifying); Rom 3:24; 8:33-34

Here is the gospel's answer to self-justification: the same verb describes the frantic self-defence of Luke 16:15 and the gift of Romans 3:24 ("justified by his grace as a gift"). We justify ourselves because no one else will; but "Who shall bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn?" (Rom 8:33-34). The fig leaf (Gen 3:7) is unnecessary when the verdict has been given as a gift. Self-justification is what the soul does when it believes no one will speak for it; the gospel is that Someone has.

4.5 A Justification Detector

AskWhat it surfaces
What am I explaining that no one has asked about?Pre-emptive defence
If the same thing were done to me, would I call it acceptable?Double standards
What would I have to admit if I stopped explaining?The protected I-am-not ("then I would be bad / worthless")
Can I say "I was wrong" and, in the next breath, "and I am still held"?Whether identity is settled enough to bear accountability
